set.hook: A Moda wine bar pouring only Turkish bottles, nearly all of them by the glass through Coravin.
set.why: Wayana took over the room in Moda where Cenap Kuzuoğlu had run BEPPE, a pizzeria the neighbourhood was sorry to lose, and reopened it as a bar that sells nothing but Turkish wine. The trick is the Coravin: a needle draws wine through the cork, so a bottle of some rare Anatolian grape can be poured a glass at a time without being opened. Reviewers name Cenap and Asuman as the owners behind the list.
set.caveat: Address differs across listings (Ferit Tek Sok. 60/B; General Asım Gündüz Cad. 24; Moda Cad.) - check the map pin before walking

set.hook: Kadıköy's long-running club and garden bar on Kadife Sokak, the room that later spawned a Berlin sibling.
set.why: Arkaoda opened on Kadife Sokak in 1999, and it travelled: its Berlin offshoot at Karl-Marx-Platz still bills itself as the child of the Kadıköy club. That says something about the original, a bar run more like a collective than a business, where the selectors drift from Turkish psych to jazz to electronic over a single night. Come for the garden in the early evening and stay for whoever is on the decks.

set.hook: Kadife Sokak's original bar, in a wooden house since 1996, with vinyl nights in the upstairs rooms.
set.why: Karga opened in 1996 in a nineteenth-century wooden house on Kadife Sokak, and the street's whole bar scene grew up around it. The building nearly ended the story early: a fire in 1998 gutted it, and the bar reopened that July. Upstairs, the small rooms run on vinyl. Its future is now the open question, because the bar's own page flagged it as closing in 2026 while it was still posting nights in August.

set.hook: Five floors off Nevizade, each with its own crowd, ending on a rooftop that leans to techno.
set.why: Şahika stacks five floors above Nevizade Sokak, the meyhane alley behind the fish market, and each level keeps its own idea of a night. The lower floors are for drinking and talking; the roof is where the programme turns experimental, with techno, jungle and footwork, and where the venue has made its name as a queer-friendly fixture. Go up late, after dinner in the alley below.

set.hook: A guitarist's jazz club below the Galata Tower, named for a Miles Davis tune, with sets most nights.
set.why: The guitarist Önder Focan and his wife Zuhal opened Nardis in October 2002 and named it after 'Nardis', the tune Miles Davis wrote for a Cannonball Adderley record. Focan still plays here with his own trio, and the bookings go to a family email address. Music starts at 21:30. The club ran a London pop-up for its twentieth anniversary, and this summer's bill went from swing sets to local singers.
set.hours: Music from 21:30, doors 21:00 (Cornucopia, Aug 2026); closing times and Sunday opening differ between sources - call ahead

set.hook: Kadıköy's home-grown roaster, up a flight of stairs above the market streets on Muvakkıthane Caddesi.
set.why: Montag began as one small shop with a roaster in Kadıköy and grew from there into a separate roasting plant and a handful of cafés, which is why so many of the city's newer bars buy from it. The original room is easy to miss: it sits on the first floor above the market lanes, small enough that a free table at a busy hour is luck. Order a filter and watch the street from above.

set.hook: A Bosphorus village of wooden houses where a mosque, a synagogue and two churches share a few streets.
set.why: Kuzguncuk's best-known corner is a mosque standing in the grounds of an Armenian church: Surp Krikor Lusavoriç opened in 1861 across from the ferry landing, and the Kuzguncuk Camii was built beside it in 1952, partly with money the Armenian community gave. A few streets inland, the Beth Ya'akov synagogue of 1878 still holds Saturday services, and the Greek church of Ayios Yeorgios is close by. Walk İcadiye Caddesi uphill and back.

set.hook: A waterside walk past Arnavutköy's wooden yalı and fishing pier, south along the shore road to Bebek's bay.
set.why: Arnavutköy sits on the European shore between Ortaköy and Bebek, and the walk joins two very different villages. One is a row of wooden Ottoman houses and a working fishermen's pier with cobbled lanes behind; the other is a curved bay of moored boats and cafés. The current is strongest at the point between them, where the water runs fast close to the path. Allow two to three hours if you stop.

set.hook: The largest Princes' Island: no cars, wooden mansions and a hilltop monastery, a ferry ride from the city.
set.why: Büyükada is the biggest of the Princes' Islands, about five kilometres by one, and private cars are kept off it, so the island moves on foot, bicycle and electric carts. Ferries leave from Kabataş, Eminönü, Kadıköy and Bostancı. Most walkers aim for the Monastery of St George on the higher of the two hills, a steady climb from the wooden houses near the pier. Take an early boat back on a Sunday.
set.caveat: Ferry times change with the season: the 2026 summer timetable ran 29 June to 6 September; check sehirhatlari.istanbul for the current one

set.hook: The Asian-side ferry town where the city's food market, bar streets and Moda's seafront all meet.
set.why: Kadıköy is a ferry town first: most people arrive by boat, and the market grid starts a few minutes uphill from the pier, with fishmongers who were cutting cheap hand-line palamut until evening this August. Beyond it the bar streets around Kadife Sokak keep going past midnight, and Moda's seafront park takes the sunset. The district is changing fast; rents have pushed out small businesses, and police raided bars in April 2026.

set.hook: A Karaköy deli counter by the ferry, cutting pastırma and cheese for the boat from seven in the morning.
set.why: Namlı is a family charcuterie house, and its Karaköy shop, opened in 2007, works as both deli and breakfast room a few steps from the ferry. Its own online store prices everything, which makes it an honest benchmark: in August 2026 scraped-crust pastırma was ₺5,400 a kilo and Gelibolu eski kaşar ₺1,690. Come early: weekend breakfast fills the tables, but the counter keeps cutting while you wait.

set.hook: The 1871 coffee house by the Spice Bazaar where the queue buys Turkish coffee ground while it waits.
set.why: Mehmet Efendi took over his father's shop on Tahmis Sokak in 1871 and started selling coffee already roasted and ground, which is how the family got the name kurukahveci, dry-coffee seller. The building the company stands in now is its own landmark, credited to the architect Zühtü Başar. The firm exports to more than sixty countries, but the counter grind is only sold in its own three shops.

set.hook: Antep baklava from a family counter in Karaköy, baked in the house's own workshop on Mumhane Caddesi.
set.why: The baklava sold here is baked a street away, in the workshop the family set up on Mumhane Caddesi in 1996, and a Güllüoğlu sign anywhere else belongs to a different company. Nadir Güllü, who chairs the firm and still works as a usta, runs it with his brother Ömer and his children. set.hook: Kadıköy's market lanes behind the pier: fishmongers, butchers, delis and greengrocers on Güneşlibahçe.
set.why: The fishing season opens on 1 September, but this August the Kadıköy fishmongers were already selling palamut caught on hand lines from small boats, at 100 lira a fish, and one of them said they were cleaning fish until evening. That is the rhythm of this street: the counters sell what came in, and the price is chalked up by the kilo. The delis, among them Gözde Şarküteri at no. 8, fill the gaps.

set.hook: A tiled 1876 boza shop below the Süleymaniye hill: boza in the cold months, şıra in the summer.
set.why: Hacı Sadık Bey came to Istanbul from Prizren and opened this shop in Vefa in 1876, and his family has kept it since. Boza is millet, fermented until it thickens and turns slightly sour, and it is a cold-weather drink, served chilled from roughly October to April with cinnamon and roasted chickpeas. In summer the counter switches to şıra, a sweet raisin drink, so the shop does not close when the season ends.
set.hours: Boza in the cold months (roughly October to April), şıra in summer; current opening hours not found - call ahead

set.hook: A Turkish and Rum meyhane on the first floor of Minoa Pera, in Vallaury's 1896 Union Française building.
set.why: The building is the draw before the meze: Alexandre Vallaury designed the Union Française in 1896, and Minoa Pera has filled it with a bookshop, a café, a bar and a stage. Perviz Resuli opened the meyhane upstairs for seventy guests, cooking the Rum side of the old city's tables. Gazete Oksijen covered the opening in November 2025, and its trading status has been unclear since.
